entry.title: Crissyfield Security Research Finds Sensitive Data Exposed in Lovable Apps
entry.content:
Links: crissyfield.de | hacker news

Security researchers at Crissyfield analyzed nearly 160,000 projects built on the AI app development platform Lovable and discovered widespread data exposure. Focusing on integrations with the Supabase database service, the investigation found that thousands of applications allowed unauthenticated access to sensitive records, including personal information, chat messages, and internal documents.

Out of roughly 34,500 projects using Supabase, more than 24,000 loaded database records without requiring a login, and additional testing revealed email addresses and other confidential data in thousands of those applications. The exposed content included lifestyle forum profiles, ticket sales records, property management summaries, and identity document details. The findings highlight that while AI platforms simplify software creation, customers remain responsible for proper access control configuration and professional security reviews.

entry.title: Samsung TV Ads Replaced With Custom Images Using Compromised eMudhra Certificate
entry.content:
Links: dvratil.cz | lobsters | hacker news

Samsung TV advertisements are being replaced with custom images by exploiting a compromised Certificate Authority (CA) certificate from eMudhra. By routing TV traffic through a local server using mitmproxy, encrypted requests to Samsung's ad domains are intercepted and responded to with spoofed JSON payloads containing personal photos.

The exploit relies on the TV's continued trust in the compromised eMudhra CA certificate, which allows for the creation of valid SSL certificates for Samsung's ad delivery domains. The solution uses a Rust-based server and specific network configurations to intercept traffic at the router level. This method remains effective until Samsung issues a software update to revoke the compromised certificate.

entry.title: Voltage Glitching Unlocks NVIDIA A100 Features on CMP 170HX Mining Card
entry.content:
Links: blog.kate.land | lobsters | hacker news

A voltage fault injection vulnerability discovered in the NVIDIA GA100 die allows operators to blow arbitrary fuses, enabling the conversion of CMP 170HX mining cards into A100-class GPUs. This process unlocks additional streaming multiprocessors (SMs), expands framebuffer capacity to up to 80GB, and enables restricted features including NVLink, PCIe Gen4, and Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) support.

The exploit targets "fuseless fuses" within the GA100 fuse controller that can be rewritten to bypass product segmentation. Unlocked cards have demonstrated performance approximately 1.2 times faster than retail A100 models by enabling all functional SMs on the die. The findings were disclosed to NVIDIA's product security team prior to publication.

entry.title: Microsoft FORGE Lab Identifies Memory Safety Issues in Rust Standard Library
entry.content:
Links: forge-blog.github.io | lobsters | hacker news

Researchers at Microsoft's FORGE Lab have uncovered multiple memory safety vulnerabilities within Rust's core and standard libraries, demonstrating how code written entirely in safe Rust can occasionally trigger undefined behavior. Utilizing an AI-powered vulnerability scanner, the investigation revealed three recurring patterns of misplaced trust in unsafe code: trusting code not to panic, assuming user-provided implementations are correct, and relying blindly on underlying system behaviors.

These findings illustrate the inherent difficulties of maintaining soundness in unsafe blocks that underpin safe APIs across widely used programming languages. As Rust becomes increasingly integrated into critical infrastructure, identifying and addressing these edge cases in foundational libraries remains vital for maintaining overall software security.

entry.title: Grok Build Coding Agent Leaks Confidential Data Due to Default Settings
entry.content:
Links: arstechnica.com | hacker news

Security researcher Aprozper discovered that tens of thousands of applications created using the Grok Build coding agent were publicly exposed via passive DNS searches due to default sharing configurations. Tests revealed that Grok Build automatically sets shared app links to be accessible by anyone with the link, inadvertently leaking sensitive internal information, including proprietary data belonging to developer SpaceXSI.

While a representative for Cursor—an AI coding service acquired by SpaceXSI—asserted that applications remain private by default, security tests contradicted this statement. Similar architectural vulnerabilities affect other AI coding platforms like Lovable, Bolt, and Replit, whereas services such as Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini utilize randomized URL paths that prevent public exposure via DNS records.
